item.title: Police, protesters clash in Sydney as Israeli president’s visit sparks unrest
item.description:
Police and protesters clashed violently in central Sydney on Monday evening during demonstrations against Israeli President Isaac Herzog's visit to Australia, with 27 people arrested and at least nine facing criminal charges, including allegations of assaulting officers.

Approximately 6,000 people gathered at Sydney's Town Hall for what organizers, the Palestine Action Group, described as a peaceful rally opposing Herzog's four-day trip to Australia. As speeches concluded, demonstrators expressed their intention to march toward the NSW Parliament, defying protest restrictions that had been imposed under emergency powers following December's Bondi Beach terror attack.

item.title: Data center electricity demand to triple by 2035, new study finds
item.description:
The world's data centers are poised to consume roughly three times their current electricity by 2035, driven by the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing, according to new industry projections. Renewable energy and nuclear power are expected to supply the majority of this increased demand, even as grid infrastructure struggles to keep pace.

A report from Precedence Research published this week projects that global data center electricity consumption will climb from approximately 460 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2024 to more than 1,300 TWh by 2035. BloombergNEF's December 2025 forecast similarly estimated that U.S. data center power demand alone will reach 106 gigawatts by 2035, up from 40 gigawatts today—a nearly threefold increase.

item.title: Carney says call with Trump on Gordie Howe Bridge was 'positive'
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with President Donald Trump on Tuesday morning about the Gordie Howe International Bridge after Trump threatened to block its opening, describing the conversation as "positive" and expressing optimism the matter would be resolved.

The call came after Trump declared on his Truth Social platform Monday evening that he would "not permit" the bridge linking Windsor, Ontario, to Detroit, Michigan, to open until the United States is "fully compensated for everything we have given" Canada. Trump also demanded the U.S. receive ownership of "at least one half of this asset."

item.title: Trump considers second carrier if Iran talks fail
item.description:
The United States and Iran held their first nuclear negotiations since the 12-day war in June 2025, meeting indirectly in Muscat, Oman on February 6 with Omani officials serving as intermediaries. The talks mark a potential thaw after months of heightened tensions, though major disputes over uranium enrichment remain unresolved.

President Donald Trump described the discussions as "very good" and committed to further rounds of talks, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called them "a good start," despite acknowledging that significant work remains to establish trust between the two nations. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei characterized the half-day meeting as "a way to measure the seriousness of the other side" and to determine how the process could continue.

item.title: Pulsar discovery near Milky Way's center could test Einstein's relativity
item.description:
A flurry of findings from international research teams is prompting astronomers to reconsider long-held assumptions about the Milky Way's center and the nature of cosmic cataclysms observed by space telescopes.

A study published this week in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society proposes that the object at the heart of our galaxy may not be a supermassive black hole at all, but rather an ultra-dense clump of exotic dark matter. The research challenges the prevailing theory that Sagittarius A* — long believed to be a black hole with roughly 4 million times the mass of the Sun — is responsible for the extreme orbits of nearby stars racing at thousands of kilometers per second.

item.title: UC Irvine scientists engineer enzyme for rapid RNA synthesis
item.description:
Scientists at the University of California, Irvine have developed an engineered enzyme capable of synthesizing RNA with unprecedented speed and precision, a breakthrough that could accelerate the production of mRNA vaccines and RNA-based therapeutics.

The enzyme, dubbed C28, can produce RNA at near-natural speeds—approximately three nucleotides per second—while maintaining greater than 99% accuracy, according to research published in Nature Chemical Biology and announced by the university on Sunday. The study was led by John Chaput, a UC Irvine professor of pharmaceutical sciences.

item.title: AST SpaceMobile unfolds largest satellite antenna in LEO
item.description:
AST SpaceMobile announced Tuesday that it has successfully completed the unfolding of its BlueBird 6 satellite, now the largest commercial communications array ever deployed in low Earth orbit. The milestone positions the Texas-based company to advance its mission of delivering cellular broadband directly to standard smartphones from space.

The satellite's phased array antenna spans approximately 2,400 square feet and is designed to support peak data speeds of up to 120 Mbps, offering roughly ten times the bandwidth capacity of the company's earlier BlueBird 1-5 satellites. BlueBird 6 is also more than three times larger than those previous spacecraft.

item.title: TikTok owner ByteDance in talks with Samsung to make AI chip
item.description:
ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok, is developing its own artificial intelligence chip and is in negotiations with Samsung Electronics to manufacture it, according to people familiar with the matter, as the Chinese technology giant seeks to secure access to advanced processors amid global semiconductor supply constraints.

The Beijing-based company aims to receive sample chips by the end of March and plans to produce at least 100,000 units this year, designed primarily for AI inference tasks, Reuters reported on Tuesday. Production could eventually scale up to 350,000 units, with negotiations with Samsung also including potential access to memory chips, which remain in limited supply as companies worldwide expand AI infrastructure.

item.title: China tests Long March-10 rocket in key step toward 2030 moon landing
item.description:
China conducted a successful flight test of its Long March-10 carrier rocket and Mengzhou crewed spacecraft on Wednesday, marking a milestone in the country's ambitious plans to land astronauts on the moon by 2030. The test, which launched from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan Province at 11:00 a.m. Beijing Time, achieved multiple firsts for China's human spaceflight program.

The mission combined a low-altitude demonstration flight for the Long March-10 rocket with a maximum dynamic pressure abort test for the Mengzhou spacecraft—simulating the most dangerous moment during launch when aerodynamic stress peaks. Both the rocket's first-stage body and the spacecraft's return capsule splashed down safely in the sea in a controlled manner, according to the China Manned Space Agency.

item.title: Climate change made deadly Patagonia fires 3 times more likely, study finds
item.description:
Human-caused climate change made the hot, dry conditions that fueled recent devastating wildfires in Chile and Argentina up to three times as likely, according to a new analysis published Wednesday by the World Weather Attribution network of scientists.

The blazes that tore through Chile's Biobío and Ñuble regions in mid-January killed 23 people, destroyed more than 1,000 homes, and forced over 52,000 to evacuate. In Argentine Patagonia, fires consumed more than 45,000 hectares by early February, displacing at least 3,000 people across communities including El Hoyo, Puerto Patriada, and Epuyén.

item.title: 10 dead, including shooter, in British Columbia school shooting
item.description:
A mass shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School in northeastern British Columbia on Tuesday afternoon has left ten people dead, including the suspected shooter, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Approximately 25 additional individuals are being assessed for injuries at a local medical center, marking one of the deadliest school shootings in Canadian history.

The RCMP confirmed that officers responded to reports of an active shooter at the school at approximately 1:20 p.m. local time on February 10. During their search of the building, police located six victims deceased inside the school, along with an individual believed to be the shooter who died from what appears to be a self-inflicted injury.

item.title: Netanyahu urges Trump to expand Iran talks beyond nuclear program
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to meet President Donald Trump at the White House on Wednesday to push for a tougher U.S. stance on Iran's ballistic missile program, arriving just days after Washington resumed direct talks with Tehran for the first time since last year's 12-day war.

Netanyahu's visit marks his seventh face-to-face meeting with Trump since the president took office in January 2025, and his sixth on American soil. The Israeli leader moved up the trip from an originally scheduled February 18-19 visit after U.S. and Iranian officials held nuclear talks in Muscat, Oman on February 6. "I will present to the president our perspectives on the essential principles of the negotiations," Netanyahu told reporters before departing Israel on Tuesday, adding that these principles are "crucial not only for Israel but for anyone who desires peace and security in the Middle East."

item.title: Study links climate change to declining southern right whale births
item.description:
Southern right whales in Australian waters are having calves less often, with new research revealing that climate change is undermining decades of conservation progress for a species once celebrated as a marine recovery success story.

A major study published February 11 in Scientific Reports found that calving intervals among western Australian southern right whales have increased from an average of three to four years, meaning fewer calves are being born each year. The research, drawing on more than three decades of photo-identification data collected at the Head of the Great Australian Bight, links the reproductive slowdown to declining Antarctic sea ice, changes in oceanic conditions, and reduced availability of prey such as krill.

item.title: CME Group explores world's first rare earth futures contract
item.description:
CME Group is developing what would become the first futures contract for rare earth elements, according to three sources with knowledge of the matter who spoke to Reuters on Tuesday. The planned contract would combine neodymium and praseodymium—two critical materials used in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, fighter jets, and drones—giving Western governments, companies, and financial institutions a new tool to hedge exposure to a market dominated by China.

Rival Intercontinental Exchange is also exploring rare earth futures but is not as advanced in its planning as CME, two of the sources said. CME declined to comment, and ICE did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: MIT develops magnetic mixer to improve 3D bioprinting
item.description:
Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology have developed a magnetic mixing device called MagMix that addresses one of the most persistent challenges in 3D bioprinting: cells sinking to the bottom of printer syringes during long print sessions. The system, published February 2 in the journal Device, maintained uniform cell distribution across more than 45 minutes of continuous printing while preserving high cell viability.

The problem is simple gravity. Cells are heavier than the hydrogel "bio-inks" that carry them, causing them to settle during printing. "This cell settling, which becomes worse during the long print sessions required to print large tissues, leads to clogged nozzles, uneven cell distribution, and inconsistencies between printed tissues," explained Ritu Raman, the Eugene Bell Career Development Professor of Tissue Engineering and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT.

item.title: Bitcoin falls below $67,000 as 'Tinkerbell effect' fades
item.description:
Bitcoin dropped below $67,000 on Wednesday, extending a sharp decline that has wiped roughly 40% from its October peak as investor confidence falters and the cryptocurrency's once-tight correlation with traditional equities weakens.

The world's largest cryptocurrency fell to approximately $66,996 early Wednesday morning before stabilizing near $67,000, according to market data. The decline marks a continuation of the sell-off that began when Bitcoin broke below the $70,000 threshold on February 5, triggering what analysts described as one of the most severe deleveraging events of the current cycle.

item.title: Trump weighs second carrier for Gulf as Iran talks resume
item.description:
President Donald Trump warned on Tuesday that the United States would have to take "something very tough" against Iran if diplomatic efforts fail, as he considers deploying a second aircraft carrier to the Middle East and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu prepares to visit Washington.

In interviews with Axios and Fox Business Network, Trump said Tehran "very much wants to reach a deal" but cautioned that failure to reach an agreement would prompt severe consequences. "Either we make a deal, or we'll have to do something very tough — like last time," Trump told Axios, referencing last June's Operation Midnight Hammer, in which US forces struck three Iranian nuclear facilities at Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan.

item.title: Trump, Netanyahu end White House talks without deal on Iran
item.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with President Donald Trump at the White House on Wednesday for roughly three hours, with Netanyahu expected to convey that the second phase of the Gaza ceasefire "is not moving," according to an Israeli source familiar with the discussions. The meeting, their sixth since Trump returned to office in January 2025, produced no definitive outcomes, Trump wrote on Truth Social afterward.

"There was nothing definitive reached other than I insisted that negotiations with Iran continue to see whether or not a Deal can be consummated," Trump wrote, signaling a focus on U.S.-Iran diplomacy rather than the stalled Gaza framework.

item.title: Italy approves bill allowing naval blockades against migrant boats
item.description:
Italy's cabinet on Wednesday approved a bill authorizing naval blockades to halt migrant boats during periods of "exceptional pressure" at the nation's borders, a government source told Reuters. The legislation marks one of the most aggressive measures yet by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing government to curb irregular migration by sea.

Under the draft law, the Italian government could prohibit vessels from entering territorial waters for up to six months in cases involving serious threats to public order or national security. Violators would face fines of up to €50,000, with repeat offenders risking confiscation of their vessels—a provision widely seen as targeting charity-operated rescue ships.

item.title: NASA detects water and organic molecules on interstellar comet
item.description:
A cosmic wanderer from beyond our solar system is offering scientists an unprecedented window into how planets form around distant stars. Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, only the third confirmed interstellar object ever observed, has yielded a bounty of discoveries including the first detection of water activity from such an object, along with organic molecules and a distinctive carbon-rich composition that is reshaping our understanding of planetary building blocks across the galaxy.

The findings, announced in studies published this week, suggest that the chemical ingredients for life may be common throughout the cosmos. "When we detect water — or even its faint ultraviolet echo, OH — from an interstellar comet, we're reading a note from another planetary system," said Dennis Bodewits, professor of physics at Auburn University. "It tells us that the ingredients for life's chemistry are not unique to our own."
